topicOverview: Grade 11 Functions studies relations and function rules, their domains and ranges, operations and inverses, common families, graphs, and applications. Read a function as a relationship between inputs and outputs, and state restrictions and units when interpreting a model.

subtopics.name: Relations

definitions.meaning: Any association between elements of an input set and elements of an output set; it can be represented by ordered pairs, a table, a mapping diagram, a graph, or an equation.
The first and second components of an ordered pair (x,y), respectively.

formulas.name: Relation as a set of ordered pairs

importantProperties: A relation may assign several outputs to one input; a function may not.
A graph represents a function of x if every vertical line intersects it at most once.
The same input-output data may be represented in several equivalent ways.
commonMistakes: Assuming every relation is a function.
Applying the horizontal line test to decide whether a graph is a function; the vertical line test is the relevant test.
Treating repeated outputs as disqualifying; different inputs may share an output.
exampleProblemTypes: Decide whether a mapping diagram defines a function.
Use a vertical line test on a graph.
Convert a table or mapping into ordered pairs.
Identify repeated inputs with conflicting outputs.

subtopics.name: Functions

definitions.meaning: A relation that assigns exactly one output to every input in its domain.
The input variable, commonly x.
The output variable, whose value depends on the input, commonly y or f(x).

importantProperties: Each domain input must have exactly one output.
Several different inputs may have the same output.
A function can be represented by a rule, table, graph, mapping, or contextual model.
commonMistakes: Thinking an output can occur only once.
Calling a relation a function when one input has two different outputs.
Ignoring a stated domain restriction.
exampleProblemTypes: Classify a relation as a function or not.
Write a rule from a verbal description or table.
Identify input and output variables in context.
Use the vertical line test.

subtopics.name: Domain and range

definitions.meaning: All permitted input values for which the function is defined.
All output values produced by inputs in the domain.

variables.meaning: denominator; exclude its zeros from the domain

importantProperties: For a graph, domain is read horizontally and range vertically.
For formulas over the reals, denominator values cannot be zero and even-root radicands must be nonnegative.
The range must be found from actual outputs, not by copying the domain.
Use interval notation or set notation and respect open and closed endpoints.
commonMistakes: Forgetting denominator zeros or radical restrictions.
Including an endpoint shown by an open circle.
Using an interval that includes values outside a graph's plotted extent.
Confusing x-values with y-values.
exampleProblemTypes: Find domain restrictions from a formula.
Read domain and range from a graph or table.
Find the range of a parabola from its vertex and opening direction.
State the physical domain of a contextual model.

subtopics.name: Function notation

definitions.meaning: A naming system in which f(x) denotes the output of function f for input x.
The output associated with a particular input; for example, f(3) is one value, not f multiplied by 3.

formulas.name: Evaluate a rule at an input

importantProperties: The letter naming the function can be any symbol, such as f, g, or h.
f(x) names a value and does not indicate multiplication.
Replacing x by a number or expression means substituting the entire input.
commonMistakes: Reading f(x) as f times x.
Substituting into only one occurrence of x.
Dropping parentheses around a negative input.
exampleProblemTypes: Interpret f(4) from a table or graph.
Translate a verbal rule into function notation.
Write an output condition such as f(x)=7 as an equation.
Distinguish f(x), f(a), and f(x+h).

subtopics.name: Evaluating functions

definitions.meaning: Finding the function output for a specified input by substitution or by reading a representation.
A ratio of change in function output to change in input, often used to compare average rates of change.

importantProperties: Substitute a negative input using parentheses before simplifying.
For a table or graph, evaluation means finding the output at the stated input.
An input must belong to the function's domain for its value to be defined.
commonMistakes: Replacing x with a negative number without parentheses.
Confusing f(2) with solving f(x)=2.
Dividing by zero in a difference quotient.
exampleProblemTypes: Evaluate f(a) from a formula, table, mapping, or graph.
Evaluate f(x+h) and simplify.
Find inputs that produce a specified output.
Compute an average rate of change over an interval.

subtopics.name: Operations on functions

definitions.meaning: New functions formed by adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing the outputs of two functions at the same input.

variables.meaning: input; for the quotient also require g(x) not equal to zero

importantProperties: For sums, differences, and products, the domain is the intersection of the two input domains.
For a quotient, also exclude inputs where the denominator function g(x) equals zero.
Simplify the output expression only after applying each function to the same input.
commonMistakes: Adding the formulas but using different input values.
Forgetting the extra zero restriction for a quotient.
Assuming the product domain is the union of the original domains.
exampleProblemTypes: Find formulas for f+g, f-g, fg, or f/g.
Determine the domain of an operation on functions.
Evaluate an operation at a specified input.
Simplify an expression involving two function rules.

subtopics.name: Composition of functions

definitions.meaning: Applying one function to the output of another function.
In f(g(x)), g is applied first and f is applied to the result.

importantProperties: Composition is generally not commutative: f(g(x)) need not equal g(f(x)).
The input must be in the domain of g, and g(x) must be in the domain of f.
Composition can model a sequence of processes or unit conversions.
commonMistakes: Applying the outer function first.
Substituting g(x) for only one occurrence of the input in f.
Ignoring the intermediate domain restriction.
exampleProblemTypes: Find f(g(x)) and g(f(x)).
Evaluate a composition at a number.
Determine the domain of a composite function.
Represent a two-step process as a composition.

subtopics.name: One-to-one functions

definitions.meaning: A function in which different inputs always produce different outputs; equivalently, each output in the range comes from exactly one input.

importantProperties: A function is one-to-one exactly when every horizontal line intersects its graph at most once.
A one-to-one function has an inverse function on its range.
A function that is not one-to-one may become one-to-one when its domain is restricted.
commonMistakes: Using the vertical line test instead of the horizontal line test.
Assuming every function is one-to-one because it passes the vertical line test.
Ignoring a stated or chosen domain restriction.
exampleProblemTypes: Use the horizontal line test to classify a graph.
Show algebraically whether f(a)=f(b) forces a=b.
Choose a restricted domain that makes a function one-to-one.
Decide whether an inverse is a function.

subtopics.name: Inverse functions

definitions.meaning: The function that reverses the input-output mapping of a one-to-one function.
The relation obtained by swapping the coordinates in every ordered pair; it is not always a function.

variables.meaning: its inverse on the corresponding range

importantProperties: To find a rule, write y=f(x), interchange x and y, then solve for y.
The domain of f becomes the range of f inverse; the range of f becomes its domain.
The graphs of f and f inverse reflect across y=x.
Verify by composing in both orders on valid domains.
commonMistakes: Treating f^{-1}(x) as 1/f(x); inverse function and reciprocal are different.
Failing to restrict the domain when the original function is not one-to-one.
Forgetting to swap domain and range.
exampleProblemTypes: Find an inverse formula and state its domain.
Check whether two functions are inverses by composition.
Reflect a graph across y=x.
Find a domain restriction that permits an inverse function.

subtopics.name: Piecewise functions

definitions.meaning: A function defined by different rules on different parts of its domain.
An input value where the applicable rule or behavior changes.

variables.meaning: rules used on their stated intervals

importantProperties: Check the condition first, then substitute into only the rule whose interval contains the input.
Open and closed endpoints determine which rule applies at a breakpoint.
A piecewise function may have a jump or hole; continuity is not automatic.
Its domain is the union of the intervals where its rules are defined.
commonMistakes: Using the wrong branch for an input.
Ignoring equality in an interval condition.
Drawing both branches as including the same endpoint when only one condition includes it.
exampleProblemTypes: Evaluate a piecewise rule at inputs on different intervals.
Graph branches with open and closed endpoints.
Find the domain, range, or breakpoint outputs.
Write a piecewise model for fees, postage, or a tiered rate.

subtopics.name: Rational functions

definitions.meaning: A quotient of polynomial functions, written f(x)=p(x)/q(x), with q(x) not equal to zero.
A missing graph point caused by a common factor that cancels algebraically; the original excluded input remains outside the domain.
A line that describes graph behavior as x approaches a value or becomes very large in magnitude.

variables.meaning: denominator polynomial; its zeros are excluded from the domain

importantProperties: Find domain restrictions from the original denominator before cancelling factors.
An uncancelled denominator zero often gives a vertical asymptote; a cancelled common factor gives a hole.
If numerator and denominator degrees are equal, the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of leading coefficients.
If numerator degree is less than denominator degree, y=0 is a horizontal asymptote; if it is exactly one degree higher, polynomial division gives a slant asymptote.
commonMistakes: Treating a cancelled denominator zero as part of the domain.
Calling every denominator zero a vertical asymptote even when a common factor cancels.
Finding x-intercepts from factors that also cancel.
Assuming a graph never crosses a horizontal asymptote.
exampleProblemTypes: Find domain, intercepts, holes, and vertical asymptotes.
Determine horizontal or slant asymptotes from degrees or division.
Sketch a rational graph from its features.
Solve a rational equation and reject excluded values.

subtopics.name: Exponential functions

definitions.meaning: A function in which the variable appears in the exponent, commonly f(x)=ab^x with a not equal to zero, b>0, and b not equal to 1.
The base b that multiplies the function value for each one-unit increase in x.

variables.meaning: positive base; b>1 is growth and 0<b<1 is decay
input or number of equal time periods
rate per period as a decimal; negative for decay

importantProperties: For a>0, the basic graph passes through (0,a), has domain all real numbers, range positive outputs, and horizontal asymptote y=0.
Equal increases in x multiply the output by a constant factor.
Exponential growth is multiplicative, unlike linear growth which adds a constant amount.
A vertical shift changes the horizontal asymptote.
commonMistakes: Confusing ab^x with (ab)^x.
Using a percent rate directly instead of the factor 1+r or 1-r.
Using an annual rate with a period measured in months without converting.
exampleProblemTypes: Identify growth or decay and initial value from a formula or graph.
Build an exponential model from repeated percentage change.
Solve for an unknown time or input using logarithms.
Compare an exponential model with a linear model.

subtopics.name: Logarithmic functions

definitions.meaning: The exponent to which a positive base must be raised to produce a given positive number.
The inverse of an exponential function with base b, where b>0 and b is not equal to 1.

variables.meaning: base; positive and not equal to 1
any valid calculator base, commonly 10 or e

importantProperties: The argument must be positive; the base must be positive and not equal to 1.
Logarithmic and exponential functions with the same base are inverses and reflect across y=x.
The graph of y=log_b(x) has domain x>0, range all real numbers, and vertical asymptote x=0.
Logarithm rules apply to products, quotients, and powers, not to sums.
commonMistakes: Writing log(M+N)=log M+log N; there is no such sum rule.
Allowing a zero or negative argument in real logarithms.
Dropping restrictions after solving a logarithmic equation.
Confusing the base with the argument.
exampleProblemTypes: Convert between logarithmic and exponential form.
Expand or condense logarithmic expressions using valid rules.
Solve logarithmic or exponential equations and check restrictions.
Use logarithms to find time in a growth or decay model.

subtopics.name: Graphs and transformations

definitions.meaning: The set of ordered pairs (x,f(x)) for all x in the domain.
A change to a parent graph that shifts, reflects, stretches, or compresses it.

variables.meaning: vertical scale by |a| and reflection when negative
horizontal scale by 1/|b| and reflection when negative

importantProperties: The graph's x-intercepts solve f(x)=0; its y-intercept is f(0), when defined.
Inside changes act in the opposite direction: f(x-h) shifts right by h.
A vertical reflection occurs when the outside multiplier is negative; a horizontal reflection occurs for a negative inside multiplier.
Use domain, range, intercepts, turning points, asymptotes, and symmetry to sketch accurately.
commonMistakes: Reversing the direction of horizontal shifts.
Applying horizontal and vertical scale factors in the same way.
Drawing an asymptote as if it must never be crossed.
Plotting points outside the function's domain.
exampleProblemTypes: Sketch linear, quadratic, rational, exponential, logarithmic, or piecewise graphs.
Identify transformations from a formula.
Find intercepts, extrema, symmetry, and asymptotes.
Compare two function graphs or determine a graph's domain and range.

subtopics.name: Linear and quadratic functions

definitions.meaning: A function with constant rate of change and a straight-line graph.
A degree-two polynomial whose graph is a parabola.
The turning point of a parabola and its maximum or minimum value point.

importantProperties: A linear function has constant slope.
A quadratic opens upward for a>0 and downward for a<0.
The discriminant determines whether a quadratic has two, one repeated, or no real roots.
The vertex is on the axis of symmetry x=-b/(2a).
commonMistakes: Confusing slope with intercept.
Omitting plus-or-minus in the quadratic formula.
Confusing a vertex with a root.
Using quadratic formulas when a=0.
exampleProblemTypes: Find a line rule from points or rate and intercept.
Find quadratic roots, vertex, and intercepts.
Choose a function family from a table or graph.
Model maximum or minimum values in a contextual problem.

subtopics.name: Applications and mathematical models

definitions.meaning: A function or equation used to represent a relationship in a real situation.
An input where two modeled quantities, such as revenue and cost, are equal.
Using a model beyond the range of observed or supplied data.

variables.meaning: input values in the model domain

importantProperties: Define variables and units before selecting or building a model.
Choose a family consistent with the situation: constant rate suggests linear, a turning point may suggest quadratic, repeated percent change suggests exponential.
Restrict the domain to meaningful values such as nonnegative quantities or stated time intervals.
Distinguish interpolation from extrapolation and explain limits of a model.
commonMistakes: Using an unrealistic domain, such as negative people or items.
Confusing the input units with output units.
Interpreting a model's prediction as exact real-world certainty.
Ignoring what an intercept or maximum means in context.
exampleProblemTypes: Build a function from a cost, distance, or population scenario.
Find and interpret a break-even point.
Use a graph or formula to find a maximum or minimum.
Compare model predictions and state reasonable domain limits.
